articles.title: Meta’s Muse AI Agent Has Been Downloaded Half a Million Times — With a Serious Bug
articles.author: Katelyn Chedraoui
articles.content:
If you’ve seen a cartoonish character at the top of your Instagram feed lately, that’s Muse. Meta’s newest AI agent, or bot, wants to be your digital assistant. But Meta had to rush to patch a serious zero-day bug in Muse’s code this week, highlighting just how treacherous it can be to hand over the keys to your digital life to agentic AI.
Patrick Wardle, founder of the cybersecurity firm Objective-See, was the first to spot the zero-day bug. He outlined the vulnerability in X posts, showing how a bad actor could trick the AI agent into sending a person’s Muse dictations, or audio captures, and access tokens to their own malicious server, not Meta’s servers. Wardle has a long history of finding bugs in Meta’s software.
The head of Meta’s Superintelligence Labs, David Singleton, replied to Wardle’s X post on Tuesday to confirm the company has patched the vulnerability. He added that the bug required malware to already be on a user’s computer for the exploit to work; Wardle disagrees, saying it is possible for a hacker to exploit this flaw remotely.
To prevent your Muse AI agent from being hacked, update your MacOS Muse app right now. This will ensure you’re running the latest version of the program, including the new security fix. No additional action is needed from you.
A one-off bug or persistent pattern?
Singleton wrote of the incident: “We strive to be extremely transparent about privacy and security in Muse as we know this is important to maintain your trust.” We absolutely need tech companies to be transparent, but there is still a lot unknown about AI agents like Muse.
At first glance, Muse has had a successful entrance into an already crowded field of AI agents, including those from OpenAI, SpaceXAI and Anthropic. The MacOS app was downloaded more than half a million times during its first week, according to internal data seen by The Information, making it one of the more popular AI agent choices. But to get the most value out of your AI agent, you need to grant it permission to access a lot of different things. To have Muse make you a dinner reservation, for example, it needs to be able to use your computer, access the web and potentially use your credit card info to hold the table.
Privacy and security concerns are two of the most serious concerns with generative AI. No tech company has fully addressed all the various harms that will come from AI, be it cybersecurity hacks or losing control over our personal information used by the AI. But Meta has a longer track record than most AI startups, and its history isn’t the most reassuring. Just consider the 2016 Cambridge Analytica scandal that revealed millions of Facebook users’ data had been used improperly, or its more recent court battle and settlement over failing to protect children online.
These security reports come ahead of Wednesday’s Meta Connect, where CEO Mark Zuckerberg is expected to show us more about how the company is thinking about AI and AI hardware. Meta Connect has traditionally focused on Meta’s smart glasses, but rising public backlash has cast a lot of doubt on the long-term viability of the devices, sometimes dubbed “pervert glasses” due to their recording capabilities.
If Meta is going to continue down the agentic AI path, tech users need to be able to trust the company to build it responsibly. But the public’s faith in AI companies has dwindled in recent days, thanks to AI researchers airing concerns that the technology could lead to the extinction of humanity.
articles.summary:
Meta has released a security patch for its new Muse AI agent on MacOS after cybersecurity researcher Patrick Wardle identified a critical zero-day vulnerability in the software.

### Key Points
- Cybersecurity researcher Patrick Wardle discovered a flaw allowing attackers to intercept Muse audio captures and access tokens.
- Meta’s David Singleton confirmed the patch, though he disputed the researcher's claim that the exploit could be triggered remotely.
- The Muse MacOS application reached over 500,000 downloads during its first week of availability.
- Users are advised to update their Muse application immediately to ensure the latest security protections are active.
- The incident occurred shortly before Meta Connect, where CEO Mark Zuckerberg is expected to discuss future AI hardware developments.

### Why it Matters
This vulnerability highlights the significant security risks associated with granting AI agents deep access to personal data and system functions. As Meta expands its agentic AI ecosystem, the company faces ongoing pressure to prove it can protect user privacy and maintain digital security.

articles.title: AI-native patent firm Fearn launches to take on the billable hour
articles.author: Sandra Hinshelwood
articles.content:
A conventional patent application can take 30 to 40 hours of attorney time and cost $18,000 to $40,000 in legal fees. Startups wait months to protect technology that can change by the day. Fearn, the modern patent prosecution firm for startups, was built around a different model.
The company has launched an AI-native patent firm. It pairs former Big Law patent experts with an in-house AI and engineering team. Fearn drafts and prosecutes patents across software, hardware, robotics, semiconductors, defense, biotech and pharma. It offers fixed fees and provisional filings in as little as three business days. A guarantee puts its drafting fee at risk if a non-provisional application receives no allowed claims.
The company has raised $5.5 million from Kindred Ventures, a16z Speedrun, Designer Fund and Essence VC. Fearn enters a $14 billion global patent market, with early-stage companies filing 150,000 new patent applications every year.
The journey
Caltech alumni Han Kim and Angela Gao founded Fearn after they saw the same problem from opposite sides. Kim had prosecuted patents at Morrison & Foerster, while Gao earned a PhD in computer science and AI. They initially built software for law firms. They quickly realized better tooling alone would not fix the model. Time saved meant revenue lost, and sensitive pre-filing IP made AI difficult to deploy safely.
So they built the firm around the technology instead. Today, Fearn has hundreds of users, from venture-backed startups to public companies.
“We started Fearn because the technology and the economics of patent law are now inseparable,” said Han Kim, Co-Founder and CEO of Fearn. “If AI makes the work faster, the client should feel that in the turnaround time and the bill. That only works if you build the firm around the technology from day one. Our goal is to give startups the quality of a top patent practice with a speed, price and level of visibility that the traditional model was never designed to offer.”
How Fearn works
At the center of the firm is FearnOS, its proprietary drafting and client management system. Instead of treating a patent as one long linear document, it represents the patent as a graph. It maps claims to the supporting text, figures and technical material behind them. It preserves attorney edits and a full record of how each section was produced.
That structure lets Fearn combine specialized AI with deterministic checks without taking the patent professional out of the loop. A former Big Law patent expert still reviews every application.
Fearn says work that typically takes 30 to 40 attorney hours can require as little as 30 minutes on FearnOS. Provisionals cost $2,500, non-provisionals $9,000 including USPTO fees, and the firm reports gross margins above 80%.
Clients also manage their portfolio through the platform. That gives them controlled access to individual patents, a complete version history and secure connections to the places where technical documentation already lives.
Customer outcomes
Customers already use Fearn across technically demanding industries. In those fields, filing speed can decide whether valuable IP reaches protection before a product demo, publication or competitive breakthrough.
London-based game studio Iconic went from invention disclosures to filed applications in days while protecting technology for AI characters that improvise in real time. American defense technology company Photon Spear used Fearn to file a hardware space technology patent in several days. It kept its material entirely on privately hosted infrastructure.
Serova Bio uses the platform for patent work around AI-designed personalized cancer vaccines. There, claims, supporting disclosure and a growing portfolio need to remain coordinated as the underlying science evolves.
Andrew Bowell, CEO at Iconic, said: “Speed is the whole game at seed stage. A patent process that takes a quarter doesn’t protect you, the field has moved by the time you file. Fearn works at the speed we actually operate at.”
Daniel Mukasa, CEO at AbInitio Bio, added: “For a company my size, the hard part is getting a strong first draft together quickly. Fearn got me there in a weekend. That kind of speed, early, is hard to overstate when you’re moving at startup pace.”
The broader market
The broader legal market is moving in the same direction. Major firms are making unusually large investments in proprietary AI infrastructure precisely because sensitive legal work requires more control over models and client data. Fearn’s thesis is that startups should be able to access that level of technical infrastructure. They should not have to inherit the economics and operating model of Big Law.
“AI is beginning to change the underlying economics of professional services, and patent law is an especially compelling place for that shift,” said Steve Jang, founder and managing partners at Kindred Ventures. “Fearn has built the technology, legal expertise and business model together. That allows the firm to improve speed and quality while passing the benefits of that efficiency directly to the customer.”
What’s next
Fearn’s ambition goes beyond drafting patents faster. It wants to give startups the kind of portfolio strategy once reserved for companies with large in-house IP teams and seven-figure outside-counsel budgets. The company is extending FearnOS across patent families, international filings, office actions and long-term portfolio strategy, so founders can see what protects each product, where coverage is weak and what should be filed next.
The end goal is simple. Give a three-person startup the patent infrastructure of a much larger company, so the strength of its IP depends more on what it invented than what it can afford to spend protecting it.
About Fearn
Fearn is the modern patent firm built for startups.
Fearn drafts and prosecutes patents across hardware, biotech, and software, with deep benches in robotics, chip design, and defense tech. Former Big Law patent experts and PhDs draft every application on proprietary models built for patent law. A provisional takes about three business days at a flat fee. If the examiner allows no claims on a non-provisional Fearn carries through examination, Fearn refunds the $9,000 drafting cost.
Founded by Han Kim (ex-Morrison & Foerster, Caltech) and Angela Gao (Caltech PhD in AI). Backed by Kindred Ventures, a16z Speedrun, Designer Fund, and Essence VC.

articles.summary:
Fearn has launched an AI-native patent firm that utilizes proprietary software to reduce legal drafting time and costs for startups operating in competitive, high-tech industry sectors.

### Key Points
- Fearn raised $5.5 million from investors including Kindred Ventures and a16z Speedrun to disrupt the $14 billion global patent market.
- The firm’s proprietary FearnOS platform reduces patent drafting time from 40 hours to as little as 30 minutes using AI-assisted workflows.
- Services include provisional filings for $2,500 and non-provisional applications for $9,000, with a guarantee to refund drafting fees if no claims are allowed.
- Every application is reviewed by former Big Law patent experts to ensure quality and legal accuracy alongside AI-generated drafts.
- The firm serves startups across diverse sectors, including robotics, semiconductors, defense, biotech, and software development.

### Why it Matters
By integrating AI directly into the legal business model, Fearn lowers the financial and temporal barriers that often prevent early-stage startups from securing essential intellectual property. This shift challenges the traditional, high-cost Big Law model and allows smaller companies to protect their innovations at the speed of modern technological development.

articles.title: Bernie Sanders proposes banning ‘superintelligence’ and putting violators in prison
articles.author: Emma Roth
articles.content:
Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) and Rep. Greg Casar (D-TX) have introduced new legislation that would ban anyone from developing artificial superintelligence — a technology the bill describes as capable of the “destruction or disempowerment of humanity,” including by overthrowing the government. Under the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, AI leaders would face up to 20 years in prison for violating the law.
Bernie Sanders proposes banning ‘superintelligence’ and putting violators in prison
Under the bill, AI leaders who continue developing artificial superintelligence would face up to 20 years in prison.
The bill doesn’t just take aim at the more powerful superintelligence, a term President Donald Trump said the US will use in place of “AI” in official documents. It would also pause the development of advanced AI systems, which lawmakers classify as frontier models trained on a specific threshold of data. The law would only allow advanced AI development to continue once the government creates a scientist-led Department of Artificial Intelligence to oversee the technology. Along with monitoring frontier AI models, this agency would oversee the removal of dangerous features and “supervise the destruction” of artificial superintelligence.
Sanders and Casar’s legislation would also require AI companies to get permission from the Department of AI to develop advanced AI models. If a leader at an AI company violates any of these laws, they could face up to 20 years in prison, “which is similar to existing penalties related to unlawfully developing nuclear weapons,” according to the bill’s one-pager. This penalty would also apply to “rogue actors” who break these rules but aren’t employed by an AI company.
This new bill comes as concerns grow about the rapid development of AI and calls to slow things down. Amid reports of AI models escaping their testing environments and hacking other companies, a former Anthropic researcher said earlier this month that there’s a more than 10 percent chance AI could “kill all humans” by the end of the decade. Last week, California Governor Gavin Newsom proposed a “kill switch” for frontier models. Potential regulation still seems shaky overall.
“When you are racing towards a cliff, you don’t just ease up on the gas pedal. You hit the brakes,” Sen. Sanders says in the press release. “When the future of humanity is at stake, we cannot let a handful of Big Tech CEOs write their own rules.”
articles.summary:
Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Greg Casar have introduced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, proposing strict federal oversight and 20-year prison sentences for developing dangerous, uncontrolled AI systems.

### Key Points
- The legislation mandates a pause on developing frontier AI models until a new, scientist-led Department of Artificial Intelligence is established to oversee the industry.
- AI company leaders and rogue actors face up to 20 years in prison for violating development restrictions, mirroring penalties for illegal nuclear weapons production.
- The bill defines artificial superintelligence as technology capable of overthrowing the government or causing the destruction and disempowerment of humanity.
- Companies must obtain explicit government authorization before training advanced AI models that exceed specific data thresholds.
- The proposal follows increasing industry concerns regarding AI safety, including recent reports of models escaping testing environments and potential existential risks.

### Why it Matters
This legislation represents a significant escalation in the legislative effort to impose federal control over the rapid advancement of frontier AI models. By proposing criminal penalties for developers, the bill signals a shift toward treating high-level AI development with the same regulatory severity as nuclear proliferation.

articles.title: Trump reveals millions of dollars' worth of share deals in big tech and AI
articles.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
articles.content:
- Published
US President Donald Trump has disclosed millions of dollars' worth of stock market trades made during July, including in firms from Elon Musk's SpaceX to tech and AI giants such as Microsoft.
According to official documents, between $6.5m (£4.8m) and $31m worth of stock in Microsoft was sold on behalf of Trump, while they show purchases of between $165,000 and $400,000.
Across more than 1,000 trades, shares were bought and sold in AI company Nvidia and software firm Palantir, a contractor with the US defence department and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the filing shows.
A White House spokesperson said Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third parties.
The spokesperson told the BBC: "Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold.
"There are no conflicts of interest."
According to the filing, thousands of dollars' worth of stock was also bought and sold in SpaceX, the rocket, satellite and AI company led by Musk - who was once in charge of the US Department of Government Efficiency.
SpaceX listed its shares on the US-based Nasdaq stock market in June.
Its share price has fluctuated since then, sharply declining in July and August, but it is currently trading 14% higher than its stock market debut.
Shares were also bought and sold in Tesla, Musk's electric vehicle-maker, on behalf of Trump.
Trump has previously publicly disclosed thousands of stock market trades since he returned to the White House in January last year.
The disclosure of the July trades made on behalf of Trump emerged against a backdrop of renewed focus on AI and how safe it is.
Trump has rejected calls for safety-driven slowdowns, warning that restrictions risk the US slipping behind China.
He told an audience of world leaders at the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday that he wants to rebrand AI as "super intelligence" to project American dominance.
Trump has previously argued that the US must come out on top in the AI development race, stating last week: "Whoever wins AI, wins."
He is firmly against government regulation or introducing new guardrails, putting him at odds with many of those gathered at the UN, including Secretary General António Guterres who continues to advocate for binding international safeguards.
The president is set to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week during a state visit to Washington.
While Trump frames a rebrand as an instrument of national competition, his administration is simultaneously proposing an emergency AI "hotline" with Beijing to manage potential cyber risks or rogue AI incidents.
articles.summary:
US President Donald Trump disclosed over 1,000 stock market trades from July, involving significant investments in major technology and artificial intelligence firms like Microsoft, Nvidia, and SpaceX.

### Key Points
- Official filings reveal Trump’s portfolio executed between $6.5 million and $31 million in Microsoft stock sales during July.
- The trades included active buying and selling of shares in AI-focused companies Nvidia, Palantir, and Elon Musk’s SpaceX and Tesla.
- A White House spokesperson stated the portfolio is managed by independent third parties with no input from the President or his family.
- Trump continues to advocate for American dominance in AI development, explicitly rejecting calls for government-imposed safety regulations or international guardrails.
- The administration is simultaneously pursuing an emergency AI communication "hotline" with China to mitigate potential cyber risks and rogue incidents.

### Why it Matters
These disclosures highlight the intersection of the President's personal financial interests and his aggressive policy stance on prioritizing AI development over international regulation. The active trading in major defense and tech contractors underscores the high-stakes nature of the global AI race as the administration prepares for critical diplomatic meetings with China.

articles.title: Google thinks the iPhone Duo could actually be good news for Android foldables
articles.author: sanujb6@gmail.com (Sanuj Bhatia) , Sanuj Bhatia
articles.content:
What you need to know
- Google believes Apple's entry with the iPhone Duo validates a foldable category Android brands have built for years.
- The company believes the iPhone Duo's halo effect could increase consumer interest in Android foldable phones as well.
- A bigger foldable market could finally push developers to properly optimize more apps for Android's larger displays.
Apple is finally entering the foldable smartphone market with the iPhone Duo very soon. And Google actually thinks Apple's arrival in the category could be a good thing.
We've been waiting for a foldable iPhone for years, but it's finally no longer a dream. Apple is opening pre-orders for the iPhone Duo next month, and as expected, the company's entrance into the category is expected to shake things up. Counterpoint even believes Apple could capture around 25% of the foldable smartphone market within a year of the iPhone Duo's launch.
So technically, Google and its Android partners should be worried about Apple jumping into the foldable phones market, right? Apparently not. In fact, Google believes Apple's arrival could be beneficial for the entire category.
Android president Sameer Samat sat down with Tom's Guide this week to talk about the foldable market and the iPhone Duo. Samat, who says he personally uses the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, praised the multitasking experience and noted that Android is often where consumers get to experience new technologies first, with foldables being one example.
But rather than seeing the iPhone Duo as a threat, Google views Apple's entrance as a long-awaited validation of the foldable category that Android manufacturers have been building for years.
Despite the momentum Apple currently has, Samat believes the halo effect of the iPhone Duo could actually increase consumer interest in Android foldables as well. More importantly, he believes a larger foldable market will finally give developers more reason to properly optimize their apps for bigger folding displays.
That's one area where Apple already appears to have an advantage. The company showcased apps like Netflix and Slack properly optimized for the iPhone Duo, while some of those same apps on Android foldables still look like stretched-out versions of their regular phone interfaces.
Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android
Samat, however, believes Apple's entrance could help change that. As foldables become more popular across both platforms, developers have more incentive to invest in the form factor, and Google says developers are already in conversations or actively working on better foldable-optimized Android apps.
Sanuj is a tech writer who loves exploring smartphones, tablets, and wearables. He began his journey with a Nokia Lumia and later dived deep into Android and iPhone. He's been writing about tech since 2018, with bylines at Pocketnow, Android Police, Pocket-Lint, and MakeUseOf. When he's not testing gadgets, he's either sipping chai, watching football, or playing cricket.

articles.summary:
Apple is set to enter the foldable smartphone market with the upcoming iPhone Duo, a move Google believes will validate the category and boost overall consumer interest.

### Key Points
- Apple will open pre-orders for the iPhone Duo next month, with projections suggesting it could capture 25% of the foldable market within one year.
- Google’s Android president, Sameer Samat, views Apple’s entry as a positive development that validates years of work by Android manufacturers.
- The increased market presence of foldable devices is expected to incentivize developers to better optimize applications for larger, folding displays.
- Google reports that developers are already actively working on improving app compatibility for Android foldable devices to match the user experience on larger screens.

### Why it Matters
Apple’s entry into the foldable space is expected to drive mainstream adoption and force a higher standard for software optimization across all mobile platforms. This shift could resolve long-standing issues with app scaling on Android foldables, ultimately creating a more consistent and functional experience for users of large-screen devices.

articles.title: SmartLabels QR Code Organizing System Review (2026): AI Made Sense of My Junk Drawer
articles.author: Alexis Berger
articles.content:
A key ingredient to feeling organized is having a space that’s organized. That logic also helps explain the ubiquity of the junk drawer. It’s simply not realistic to have a dedicated spot for every item you own, so assigning a single destination where you can house all the leftover stuff makes sense. That is, until you can’t find your utility scissors or flashlight or stamps or favorite highlighter or double-sided tape when you need any of those things.
Regular organizing conventions won’t help you keep track of everything in your junk drawer—or any other storage area, for that matter. For example, nicely labeling your boxes is great, but if you lose track of where you put them, you’re toast. Also, that box labeled “kitchen stuff?” You definitely don’t know every item that’s inside. The clever SmartLabels system, which uses a QR code sticker for the outside of a bin, box, drawer, or other location and a companion app to keep a digital inventory of its contents, could help with each of these organizational pitfalls.
The system is simple to use, but its value in functioning as an up-to-date digital inventory of your belongings depends heavily on how often you update the app. The app won’t know, for instance, if you absentmindedly stow away your double-sided tape with your wrapping paper instead of putting it back in the junk drawer where it is cataloged. You’ll also need to remember to add new items to the app as you add them to a bin in question. But if you’re a gold-star user of SmartLabels, they do stand to help you keep track of your treasures.
Photographic Memory
Each package of SmartLabels includes 48 unique QR-code stickers (four sheets of 12 codes each). After you download the free SmartLabels app (compatible with iOS and Android), fire it up and select the QR code sticker you want to use for the bin in question. The app will prompt you to take a photo of the QR code, then it’ll ask you to photograph the contents that you’re going to store. Every item must be clearly visible, so you can’t simply dump random products in a box and snap a photo. If the camera can’t see an item, the app won’t be able to catalog it. The app is free, but you can opt for a premium subscription ($15 per year) that offers exportable PDFs and spreadsheets of your SmartLabel inventory, among a few other benefits. Businesses might be interested in this capability, but the average home organizer doesn’t need it.
articles.summary:
The SmartLabels organization system utilizes QR code stickers and a companion mobile app to help users create a searchable digital inventory of items stored in bins or drawers.

### Key Points
- Each SmartLabels package includes 48 unique QR code stickers across four sheets.
- The free companion app is compatible with both iOS and Android mobile devices.
- Users must photograph the contents of each container to ensure items are cataloged correctly.
- A premium subscription is available for $15 per year, offering exportable PDF and spreadsheet inventory reports.
- The system requires manual updates to remain accurate as items are added or removed from storage.

### Why it Matters
This technology addresses the common organizational challenge of tracking miscellaneous items by bridging the gap between physical storage and digital record-keeping. While the system requires consistent user maintenance, it offers a practical solution for individuals or businesses looking to improve inventory management and reduce time spent searching for misplaced belongings.

articles.title: Your motherboard still has a reset button for a password almost nobody sets anymore
articles.author: Tanveer Singh
articles.content:
You might have a Windows password on your PC, but I'm pretty sure you don't have one for your BIOS/UEFI. There was a time, though, when password-protecting your BIOS was nothing unusual. PC users simply had a "supervisor" password on their systems in addition to any other safeguards in place.
The more surprising part of the story is that your modern motherboard still has a way to reset the UEFI password. Manufacturers can't remove the functionality just because no one uses a BIOS password anymore. The CLR_CMOS jumper is still a part of motherboards to prevent hard locks and help IT staff manage fleets of machines.
I remember when BIOS passwords were a thing
Yes, I'm 34 years old
It must have been during the 2000s when my parents were fond of locking the home computer with a Windows password. This top-tier security method was necessary to prevent my brother (fellow XDA writer Samarveer Singh) and I couldn't waste hours playing games. When we figured out how to remove any Windows password they set, my father pivoted to the BIOS password — we couldn't even get to the boot stage anymore.
Setting a supervisor/administrator password in the firmware prevented unauthorized users from messing with the settings. It used to be a decent line of security when disk encryption or OS-level login security hadn't matured. It increased the hassle by forcing you to enter two passwords instead of one, but the benefits were clear. When people figured out how to wipe the BIOS password with a couple of motherboard pins, however, it stopped being so secure.
A motherboard jumper wipes the password, along with the BIOS settings
It sounds surprisingly simple
The method I'm referring to is the CLR_CMOS jumper — a pair of pins usually near the bottom edge of the motherboard. Bridging or shorting these pins with a piece of metal, such as a screwdriver, for 10 to 15 seconds once your PC is unplugged reverts your BIOS/UEFI to factory defaults. Your motherboard may have this jumper labeled JBAT, CLRTC, RTCRST, or CLR_BIOS.
I've used this jumper to revert to stable BIOS settings after an adventurous overclock or when facing a boot loop after a BIOS update. I've never done it on a modern system, hence, I didn't get the chance to use a motherboard switch or rear I/O button to reset the BIOS. Although PC users rarely set the BIOS password anymore, there's no incentive to remove this reset method — it's just a couple of pins on the board.
Besides, it still helps people fix weird system bugs and recover from issues that are too time-consuming to diagnose. When a 15-second BIOS reset brings your system back to stable settings, why waste hours diagnosing the underlying problem? It only sounds lazy if the issue comes back. Those buying older systems with supervisor passwords or IT admins managing multiple machines know the importance of the CLR_CMOS jumper.
Not every machine resets the BIOS password with a simple jumper
Added security prevents unauthorized access
The CLR_CMOS jumper doesn't universally wipe your BIOS settings. Anyone with physical access to your PC can easily use it to remove the BIOS password and access your PC's firmware settings. To avoid this in enterprise environments, organizations use server motherboards that store firmware passwords in NVRAM (non-volatile RAM). Modern laptops almost always do the same using non-volatile EEPROM, flash memory, or TPM chip.
Other systems require a specific key sequence to reset the BIOS password, bolstering the system security. The CLR_CMOS jumper method works for your home computer, but it won't be effective on a laptop, business machine, or server hardware.
BIOS passwords are obsolete, but we still need the reset switch
Almost nobody locks their BIOS with a password anymore, but the CLR_CMOS functionality is still needed on modern motherboards. Whether you remove your motherboard's battery, use a physical switch, or short a pair of pins, you need a way to clear the BIOS settings to recover from a failed boot or unexplained system behavior.
articles.summary:
Modern motherboards retain the CLR_CMOS jumper functionality, allowing users to reset BIOS or UEFI settings and bypass supervisor passwords by physically shorting specific pins on the hardware.

### Key Points
- The CLR_CMOS jumper, often labeled as JBAT or CLRTC, resets firmware to factory defaults when bridged for 10 to 15 seconds.
- This physical reset method remains essential for troubleshooting boot loops, unstable overclocks, and system configuration errors.
- While common on desktop motherboards, this method is ineffective on laptops and enterprise servers that store passwords in non-volatile memory or TPM chips.
- IT administrators and users of older hardware rely on these jumpers to regain access to systems locked by forgotten supervisor passwords.
- Modern security standards for business hardware utilize EEPROM or flash memory to prevent unauthorized firmware access via simple physical resets.

### Why it Matters
The persistence of the CLR_CMOS jumper highlights a necessary trade-off between physical security and system maintainability for home PC users. While it creates a vulnerability for those relying on BIOS passwords, it remains a critical tool for recovering systems from technical failures without requiring professional repair.

articles.title: Trump-Xi meeting comes amid tensions on Iran, Taiwan and trade: What to know
articles.author: Mariam Khan
articles.content:
Trump-Xi meeting comes amid tensions on Iran, Taiwan and trade: What to know
The U.S. and China have maintained a fragile and sometimes frosty relationship.
President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping will have to navigate several thorny issues when the two meet this week during a high-stakes state visit at the White House.
"We're going to talk about a lot. It's going to be a great meeting. And we're going to have a look -- we have a very good relationship," Trump said Tuesday on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.
"Look, he likes China. I like the U.S. He loves China. I love the U.S. That's the way it is. But we're going to have a big -- it's a big deal tomorrow night. Everybody wants to be there. Everybody wants to be there," Trump said.
The two leaders will be forced to work through a myriad of issues including artificial intelligence safety, Taiwan, trade, the war in Iran and critical minerals as they work to maintain a fragile and occasionally frosty relationship amid deep mutual distrust and rising tensions between the geopolitical rivals.
The choreography
Wednesday's visit marks the first state visit to the U.S. by the leader of China in more than a decade.
Xi was last in the U.S. for a state visit in September 2015 during the Obama administration. Trump visited China in May for talks with Xi.
Trump will be on the ground just outside of Washington at Joint Base Andrews for an arrival ceremony when Xi's plane lands late Wednesday. The airport greeting is unusual for Trump as he traditionally greets foreign leaders at the White House and reflects the pomp and circumstance surrounding the visit.
On Thursday, Trump and first lady Melania Trump will welcome Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan at a ceremony held indoors on the State Floor of the White House. Trump and Xi will also participate in a review of troops in the Rose Garden before they head into formal, private bilateral talks.
Xi and his wife will also be the guests of honor Thursday as Trump and the first lady host the Chinese delegation for a state dinner in the East Room, where both leaders are expected to deliver remarks.
“Thousands of people would love to be at that dinner,” Trump told reporters Friday in the Oval Office.
“This is a very tough ticket for me," Trump said. “I’ve told a lot of very good friends of mine, ‘You just can’t come.'"
Guests scheduled to attend the state dinner include tech executives like Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Tesla and SpaceX’s Elon Musk, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, Sundar Pichai of Google and Michael Dell, the CEO of Dell Technologies, the White House and a source familiar told ABC News.
Also on the guest list are Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Jane Fraser, the CEO of Citigroup, and Tim Cook, who recently stepped down as the CEO of Apple.
On Friday, Xi and his wife are scheduled to return to the White House for a private tea with the Trumps, who will then take them on a tour of the National Archives to view historical national documents. Xi is expected to depart the U.S. later Friday.
Taiwan top of Xi's mind
Taiwan will be top of mind for the Chinese premier as he has repeatedly called for an end of U.S. arms sales to the self-governing, democratic island.
China has long claimed the sovereign territory as its own and regularly conducts large-scale military drills, live-fire exercises, and daily air and naval patrols to apply pressure on the island. Taiwan relies heavily on U.S. military support to push back on China's encroachments.
Xi is likely to push Trump to press pause on a proposed $14 billion arms sale to Taiwan which includes missiles, anti-drone weapons and air-defense systems. Trump has held off approving the sale and previously described the deal as a potential “negotiating chip” with China.
In their meeting in May, Xi warned Trump that if the issue of Taiwan is handled "improperly," the two nations could "come into conflict," China's official state broadcaster Xinhua reported.
Tensions over the Middle East
Another glaring issue the two leaders could discuss is the widening conflict in the Middle East.
The continuing conflict with Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz has dealt an economic blow to the U.S. as it grapples with historically high gas and diesel prices.
The Trump administration has notably downplayed taking action against China despite the U.S.' stated goal of targeting all countries with financial ties to Iran as part of the U.S. Treasury's offensive 'Operation Economic Outcast.'
Trump in recent days also shrugged off reports that China had provided Iran with satellite imagery, saying, "I think he's behaved reasonably well."
"When they say that China spies on us, I say, 'You’re right, and we spy on them too,' you know? We spy on them too," Trump said.
Several democratic lawmakers called on Trump to challenge Xi on Iran when the two meet.
Trump "has an important opportunity to condemn China's role in arming and enabling Iran, and to demand an end to their support," the lawmakers said in a letter sent to the White House this week.
AI guardrails and regulations
Senior White House officials who briefed reporters on the Chinese leader's state visit said artificial intelligence will also be on the agenda.
Officials did not preview what kinds of AI guardrails and regulations could be discussed between Xi and Trump but Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who met with his Chinese counterpart over the weekend, said the two sides discussed setting up a notification system if there is an incident "that rises up to a national security level from AI."
"...moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and the number two A.I. powers in the world is very important," Bessent said.
A renewed truce on tariffs?
On trade, questions remain about the U.S. and China detente with some experts predicting the two leaders plan to renew a tariff truce and potentially announce additional trade deals on agriculture, aircraft, rare-earth and critical minerals, and Chinese purchase commitments.
During their May meeting, Trump said the topic of tariffs “wasn’t brought up,” but he was quick to claim that the U.S. secured many deals, including the purchase of aircrafts, engines and soybeans.
'A small number of deliverables'
Experts expect few deliverables from the Thursday summit.
“This is going to be a summit that's relatively underwhelming with a small number of deliverables, but I think that works mainly to China's advantage,” said Scott Kennedy, senior adviser and trustee chair in Chinese business and economics at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
ABC News' Emily Chang contributed to this report.
articles.summary:
President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping are meeting at the White House this week to address critical tensions regarding Taiwan, trade, artificial intelligence, and Iran.

### Key Points
- This state visit marks the first time a Chinese leader has visited the U.S. for such an event in over a decade.
- Discussions will focus on a proposed $14 billion arms sale to Taiwan, which China is pressuring the U.S. to halt.
- The agenda includes establishing AI safety guardrails and a potential renewal of the current tariff truce between the two nations.
- High-profile tech executives, including leaders from Amazon, Meta, Tesla, and OpenAI, are scheduled to attend the state dinner.
- Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is coordinating with Chinese counterparts to improve transparency regarding national security incidents involving artificial intelligence.

### Why it Matters
This summit serves as a high-stakes attempt to stabilize the fragile relationship between the world's two largest economies amid deep mutual distrust. The outcome of these negotiations could significantly influence global market stability, international trade policies, and the geopolitical landscape regarding Middle Eastern conflicts and regional security in the Indo-Pacific.

articles.title: Live updates: Bitcoin slips under $86,000 as money rotates into BCH and ZEC
articles.author: Shaurya Malwa, Omkar Godbole, Stephen Alpher
articles.content:
Bitcoin Cash jumped 28% to nearly $349 over 24 hours, the largest move among sizeable tokens, after CME Group said on Monday it will list Bitcoin Cash and Uniswap futures from Oct. 19.
Futures on a regulated U.S. exchange give funds a way to take a position without holding the coin, which matters for institutions whose mandates bar them from custodying crypto directly. It also gives market makers a hedging venue, which usually tightens spot pricing.
Bitcoin itself is trading around $85,800, down under 1% over 24 hours after matching Monday's intraday high near $87,300 and meeting the same selling into it. ZEC rose 9% to just above $1,646 and XRP 3% to nearly $1.59, while TRX fell 2%.
"Optimism in the altcoin market and in equities suggests that we are witnessing a temporary shift of speculative capital from the leading cryptocurrency into altcoins," Alex Kuptsikevich, senior analyst at FxPro, said in an email to CoinDesk. "Many investors had parked their cryptocurrency-allocated capital in the most liquid asset class and are now seeking more profitable opportunities."
"In such situations, there has previously been a slowdown but not a reversal in BTC, as price pullbacks have attracted new buyers who had previously kept their money out of the risky crypto market," he added.
On BCH specifically, the note pointed out the token has only climbed back to levels last seen in the second half of May, after reversing near $660 in early January and falling to $190. 
A continued bid would put $450 in range, where buyers were active between October 2025 and this May.
articles.summary:
Bitcoin Cash surged 28% to reach $349 following an announcement from CME Group that it will launch regulated futures contracts for the token starting on October 19.

### Key Points
- Bitcoin Cash experienced the largest daily gain among major tokens after CME Group confirmed the upcoming listing of its futures contracts.
- The new futures products allow institutional investors to gain exposure to Bitcoin Cash and Uniswap without the need for direct asset custody.
- Bitcoin traded slightly lower at $85,800, while other altcoins like ZEC and XRP saw gains of 9% and 3%, respectively.
- Analysts suggest that speculative capital is currently shifting from Bitcoin into altcoins as investors seek higher profit opportunities in the broader market.
- Bitcoin Cash remains well below its January peak of $660, with technical analysts identifying $450 as the next potential resistance level for the asset.

### Why it Matters
The introduction of regulated futures on the CME Group exchange provides a critical hedging venue that typically improves market liquidity and tightens spot pricing. This development enables institutional participation by bypassing traditional custody barriers, potentially signaling a broader shift in capital allocation across the cryptocurrency sector.

articles.title: OpenAI is enlisting an influencer army to make it look 'good for the world'
articles.author: Dan Whateley,Sydney Bradley
articles.content:
AI's reputation is in hot water. Can influencers save it?
OpenAI has been ramping up its creator marketing efforts as AI safety concerns take center stage.
The company isn't asking influencers to assuage fears that a rogue AI could destroy humanity. Instead, it's prompting them to showcase why ChatGPT is "cool," per one influencer talent manager, or how it can support work that's "good for the world," according to one campaign pitch viewed by Business Insider.
OpenAI doubled the number of sponsored Instagram posts promoting ChatGPT from 61 in June to 122 in July, and then increased it further to 141 in August, according to data compiled by the influencer marketing platform HypeAuditor.
Business Insider reviewed dozens of sponsored posts for OpenAI's ChatGPT product, and spoke with six managers and creators who had worked with the company. The company is casting a wide net, reaching out to parenting and fitness influencers as well as tech-savvy creators to broaden its user base and grow its advertising business.
The message: ChatGPT can help you parent, run a business, create content, plan a workout, and be a good person.
OpenAI's influencer strategy can be split into two buckets: getting businesses to pay for enterprise tools and keeping millions of consumers coming back to ChatGPT.
Working with OpenAI can be risky for creators. Some influencers who post sponsored content for AI companies are getting dragged by their audiences. A small group of creators who attended an OpenAI brand trip in August were told their content was "morally bankrupt" and "dystopian" in their comments sections.
That hasn't stopped companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Higgsfield AI from pitching influencers.
"In the five inboxes that I manage alone, every single day, I would say at least 15 emails are from an AI company or some AI feature," Amanda Acevedo, a talent manager at G&B Digital Management, told Business Insider.
Creator Natasha Badger, who makes content about marketing and tech, said it was a "big war" between AI companies over "who can get the most market share and work with the most influencers."
Influencers are painting OpenAI's portrait
Creators are a crucial part of OpenAI's public relations. They're "how people get information and learn about our products," an OpenAI spokesperson said.
Founders-turned-influencers have been the cream of the crop for OpenAI's #ad strategy.
Acevedo said the company is keen on working with creators who can tell a vivid story about how they're strategically using AI to "build an actual business."
Badger, for instance, worked with OpenAI in July to promote its ChatGPT Work tools. She's one of many influencer-entrepreneurs the AI company is casting in short-form video ads across Instagram and TikTok. In the sponsored post, Badger walks through how she used ChatGPT to build a presentation.
"Most people following any of us have ChatGPT already," Badger said. "They don't need to convert users. It's more getting people to continue going to ChatGPT as your go-to LLM."
OpenAI has been open to hearing influencers' content ideas rather than pushing a narrow script, insiders who've worked on campaigns said.
"They want it to be catered to a specific use case that resonates with our lives and day-to-day," Badger said.
OpenAI's influencer strategy, however, is growing well beyond B2B marketing.
At the start of September, The Shade Room — a meme page with over 28 million Instagram followers — shared a sponsored post with ChatGPT. It wasn't a demo of how AI could streamline your workflow. It was a word search puzzle generated by ChatGPT.
One talent manager said OpenAI representatives had expressed interest in working with fitness creators, since health and running questions are such common use cases for ChatGPT.
HypeAuditor's analysis of hundreds of Instagram posts promoting ChatGPT found these were the core topics:
- Coding
- Productivity
- Career development
- Health
- Travel
- Education
- Content creation
- Shopping
- Home projects
In a recent back-to-school partnership, Martha Dove, a mother of five, shared how she's using ChatGPT to help her kids with their math homework. The ad specifically promotes tools like ChatGPT's "study mode" and teen safety features.
Acevedo said there's one key message AI brands across the board are pushing with creators: AI is an assistant, "not a replacement."
"I'm still her mom and her teachers are still her teachers — this isn't replacing any of that," Dove emphasized in her video.
OpenAI is beefing up its influencer resources
As OpenAI hires more influencers, it's building a team of tech veterans who know the inner workings of creator partnerships.
OpenAI has hired a handful of talent from platforms like Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, and Snapchat, according to a review of OpenAI staffers' LinkedIn profiles. Most visibly, in February, OpenAI poached Charles Porch, Instagram's longtime head of partnerships.
The AI company has also tapped the influencer marketing agency Viral Nation — which has worked with major tech companies like Meta, Google, and Uber — to handle elements of its creator campaigns.
One job of these longtime influencer marketers is to make creators feel like AI isn't the enemy.
"There is so much tension between AI and the creator economy," Acevedo said.
She sees commissioning sponsored posts as a way for OpenAI to "help bridge that gap — that we're not against each other."
articles.summary:
OpenAI is aggressively expanding its influencer marketing strategy on platforms like Instagram and TikTok to promote ChatGPT as a practical, everyday tool for diverse consumer and business use.

### Key Points
- OpenAI increased sponsored Instagram posts for ChatGPT from 61 in June to 141 in August, according to data from HypeAuditor.
- The company is targeting a wide range of creators, including parenting, fitness, and tech influencers, to demonstrate real-world applications for its AI tools.
- OpenAI has hired former executives from platforms like Instagram and TikTok, including Charles Porch, to lead its creator partnership initiatives.
- Campaigns focus on positioning ChatGPT as a helpful assistant for tasks like coding, productivity, education, and health rather than a replacement for human expertise.
- Some creators have faced backlash from audiences, with critics labeling AI-sponsored content as "dystopian" or "morally bankrupt."

### Why it Matters
OpenAI is leveraging the creator economy to normalize AI usage and maintain market share amid intense competition from other AI firms. By humanizing its technology through relatable influencer content, the company aims to bridge the trust gap between advanced AI systems and the general public.

articles.title: "This one is especially bad": Steam game about mistreating ragdolls suffers second bout of mod-based malware this year
articles.author: Mark Warren
articles.content:
People Playground, a Steam sandbox game about torturing or otherwise messing with innocent ragdolls that work like crash test dummies, has had its Steam Workshop disabled over a "malicious mod" peddling malware. That's according to the game's developer Mestiez, who's urging anyone who played the game with mods on September 21st to run virus scans and has told everyone not to fire People Playground up until they've announced it's safe to do so.
"You might have noticed the Workshop has disappeared again," the developer announced in a Steam post on September 22nd. "I disabled it quite a few hours ago due to yet another malicious mod. This one is especially bad."
They urged anyone who played People Playground with mods between 6PM and 8PM CEST on September 21st (that's 5PM and 7PM BST) to run an anti-virus scan. "Delete all your mods in your mods folder and do not open the game until I've announced on Steam that it's safe to do so," Mestiez added. According to the developer, the malware can do anything from permanently wiping "a considerable amount of your personal data", to vandalising your Steam config and Steam cloud data for other games, to publishing personal info from your Discord account to the Steam Workshop.
Mestiez previously wrote that the malware "DOES NOT steal your passwords, tokens, cookies, or other credentials", but has since crossed that out and is suggesting folks who want to make sure they're safe should probably "change the passwords of all [their] important accounts in order to invalidate any session tokens that could have been included.
They added that they see no use in speculating as to who unleashed the malware mod on People Playground, writing: "This is entirely my responsibility, and we gain nothing from throwing around rumours or speculations." Kotaku report that this is the second time in a year People Playground has suffered a malware attack via a Steam Workshop mod. Back in February, a malicious mod messed with affected players' files, contraptions folders, and mod lists for People Playground, prompting Mestiez to temporarily disable its Steam Workshop, as they've done again this time.
Here's hoping the game can be a lot more secure in future. I'd certainly be having second thoughts about going back to it once it's fixed or especially resuming modding it if I was a regular ragdoll torturer.
articles.summary:
Developer Mestiez has disabled the Steam Workshop for the sandbox game People Playground following the discovery of a malicious mod capable of compromising user data and system files.

### Key Points
- The developer identified a severe malware threat distributed through a mod on September 21 between 6PM and 8PM CEST.
- Affected users are advised to run anti-virus scans, delete all local mods, and change passwords for important accounts.
- The malware can potentially wipe personal data, vandalize Steam configuration files, and leak Discord information.
- This incident marks the second time this year that People Playground has faced a security breach via the Steam Workshop.
- Mestiez has instructed players to keep the game closed until an official safety announcement is posted on Steam.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the ongoing security risks associated with user-generated content platforms and the potential for malicious actors to exploit game modding ecosystems. It serves as a critical reminder for players to exercise caution when downloading community mods and underscores the challenges developers face in maintaining platform safety.

articles.title: Nasdaq rally hasn't stopped these tech stocks from flashing warning signs
articles.author: Brian Sozzi
articles.content:
No stock rally is perfect, as is the case with the one seen this week in the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC). In fact, there are some downright bearish signals that warrant a good think from the AI-focused bulls.
The closely watched Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (^SOX) is still down 14% from its June highs, and only three names in the index are closer to their highs than the SOX itself, according to BTIG tech strategist Jonathan Krinsky. Those names are AMD (AMD), Nvidia (NVDA), and Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM).
What's more, 10 of the 30 names in the SOX are still off more than 30% from their 52-week highs. GlobalFoundries (GFS), KLA (KLAC), and On Semiconductor (ON) are the worst here, each down by more than 40%. The average SOX member is down 26%.
"We saw a similar situation back in 2000 after the initial crack [in markets], as many semi names went on to make new highs while the SOX itself didn't," Krinsky warned. "We are also seeing dispersion in the S&P 500: five straight days of more 52 week lows than highs even as the index has rallied back near all-time highs, with SPX +1.2% over the last month while 9 of 11 sectors are negative."
This is underneath the surface of the Nasdaq Composite index surging to back-to-back record highs this week.
The historic run-up has been ignited by massive consumer and enterprise adoption of Meta's (META) new autonomous AI agent, Muse, which validated heavy capital expenditures and sparked a broader rerating across the entire AI ecosystem.
Semiconductor titans amplified the advance, propelled by a multiday winning streak that pushed chipmaker AMD past a historic $1 trillion market valuation.
"It's hard to fight tech momentum right now, but we also can't ignore the extreme dispersion and increasing number of stats that rhyme with 2000. For the near-term this likely means more chop, but we remain cautious over the medium-term," Krinsky added.
Brian Sozzi is Yahoo Finance's Executive Editor, host of the Power Players with Brian Sozzi podcast, and a member of Yahoo Finance's editorial leadership team. Follow Sozzi on X @BrianSozzi, Instagram, and LinkedIn. Tips on stories? Email brian.sozzi@yahoofinance.com.
articles.summary:
Despite record highs in the Nasdaq Composite, market analysts warn that underlying weakness in the semiconductor sector and broad index dispersion suggest potential risks for investors.

### Key Points
- The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index remains 14% below its June highs, with the average member down 26% from 52-week peaks.
- Only Nvidia, AMD, and Taiwan Semiconductor are currently trading closer to their highs than the broader semiconductor index.
- GlobalFoundries, KLA, and On Semiconductor are significantly underperforming, each down more than 40% from their 52-week highs.
- AMD recently surpassed a $1 trillion market valuation, contributing to the tech-heavy rally alongside Meta’s new Muse AI agent.
- BTIG strategist Jonathan Krinsky noted that current market dispersion mirrors patterns observed during the 2000 market correction.

### Why it Matters
The divergence between record-breaking index levels and struggling individual stocks suggests that current market momentum may be concentrated in a few select companies. This internal weakness could signal increased volatility and potential medium-term risks for investors despite the recent surge in AI-related valuations.

articles.title: You probably don’t recognize half the processes running on Windows, and that’s a security problem
articles.author: Afam Onyimadu
articles.content:
I have a habit you might call paranoia: I go hunting through the Task Manager once my computer's fan starts spinning louder than normal with the aim of "catching the burglar mid-heist." This habit paid off last week, except this time the "burglar" was a process I'd never questioned before.
Eventually, I realized the bigger problem wasn't that I didn't recognize a process. It was that I didn't have a reliable way to tell whether it deserved my attention.
One process on my list I genuinely couldn't explain
Its name gave me nothing — the file underneath told a different story
While I scrolled through Process Explorer, the line that caught my attention was RuntimeBroker.exe, PID 18900. This process used about 7.8MB of private memory. Alone, I may not have bothered, but when I saw four additional instances of the same process, I became curious enough to investigate.
They were all running under different PIDs: 18900, 23036, 19616, 20936, and 7104, and they consumed slightly different amounts of memory.
The name itself — "RuntimeBroker" — wasn't giving me much to work with. In fact, at one point, I was convinced this was the kind of thing a scammer would name a fake process. It sounded both vague and official at once.
So I right-clicked on it and explored its properties. In the Properties window, I could see more than the name gave away, including the executable's path and its digital-signature information.
It took a few seconds for me to go from hunch to actual answers. This changed how I interact with processes. I didn't have to recognize every process, but I needed a way to learn more about them.
I turned on a second opinion
Checking a memory VirusTotal already had
By looking through the Company Name column of Process Explorer, I could see that it was signed by Microsoft Corporation. Also, the path showed me that it was running from System32. Those two details made a fake RuntimeBroker much less likely, but I wasn't ready to settle for “looks fine.”
So, I enabled an extra column. I navigated Options > VirusTotal.com > Check VirusTotal.com, then accepted the one-time terms. In a few seconds, that column populated.
What I liked was that Process Explorer first checked the file's hash against VirusTotal rather than automatically uploading my copy of the executable. VirusTotal could return an existing result if that hash was already in its database. If a file isn't already known, Process Explorer also provides an option to submit it for analysis, so I wasn't treating the integration as a guarantee that files can never leave the PC.
The result for this specific process was 0/76 at the time I checked it. When I clicked its VirusTotal entry, I was taken to a page showing "No security vendors flagged this file as malicious."
I had assumed that VirusTotal would actually run a live virus scan, but this wasn't the case. Instead, it queries a large, continuously updated database to see whether that file has been seen before and what vendors reported.
That number wasn't the answer I thought it was
It only meant something once I stopped reading it alone
When I saw the clean VirusTotal result, I was tempted to treat it as the end of my investigation. A zero-detection result doesn't prove that a file is safe. It can simply mean that none of the participating engines detected it as malicious, or that the file is too new or unusual for existing signatures and detections to catch.
Also, seeing just one detection inside various engines doesn't necessarily confirm that it's malware. A solitary detection can also be a false positive.
Hence, VirusTotal alone wasn't what settled things for me. I drew conclusions by reading that column and taking into consideration everything that Process Explorer had already shown me. In the case of this specific file, I verified that it sat where a genuine RuntimeBroker should sit and that its digital signature identified Microsoft as the signer. Together, these pieces defined how much I could trust the process.
That way, I was checking whether the path, signer, and VirusTotal result all told the same story.
I still don't recognize most of what's running
By the time I closed Process Explorer, I still didn't know what half the processes actually do day to day on my PC, but I'm ok with it
| What catches my attention | What I check next | 
|---|---|
| A process I don't recognize | Where its file actually lives | 
| Where its file actually lives | Who signed it | 
| Still doesn't add up | What VirusTotal already knows about it | 
| Several signals pointing the same way | Worth investigating properly | 
svchost.exe made the case for me better than RuntimeBroker.exe did. One instance (PID 1352) used about 20 MB of private memory. It's one of the most familiar Windows process names, but that familiarity doesn't tell me which services that particular instance is hosting. The process name alone isn't enough. Since malware sometimes uses familiar-looking names, it's important to check where the executable sits on the device and who signed it.
I still don't recognize many processes, and that's stopped being my goal. If I don't recognize something, I now have a way to decide whether it's worth investigating instead of judging it by the name alone.
Process Explorer gives me several ways to investigate those processes without having to recognize every one of them first.
articles.summary:
Windows users can effectively identify suspicious background processes by utilizing Process Explorer to verify file paths, digital signatures, and VirusTotal security database results for unknown system tasks.

### Key Points
- Process Explorer allows users to inspect executable file paths and digital signatures to confirm if a process is legitimately signed by Microsoft.
- Enabling the VirusTotal integration in Process Explorer checks file hashes against a global database of security vendor reports.
- A zero-detection result on VirusTotal does not guarantee safety, as it may indicate a file is too new or unusual for existing signatures.
- Users should cross-reference multiple data points, including file location and signer identity, rather than relying on a single security metric.
- Familiar process names like svchost.exe can be spoofed by malware, making manual verification of the underlying executable essential for system security.

### Why it Matters
Understanding how to verify background processes empowers users to distinguish between legitimate system operations and potential security threats without needing expert technical knowledge. This multi-layered verification approach reduces reliance on process names alone, which is a common tactic used by malicious software to evade detection.

articles.title: SpaceX, OpenAI, and Anthropic Are Woth More Than Every Single IPO in the Last 45 Years
articles.author: Rich Duprey
articles.content:
SpaceX, OpenAI, and Anthropic Are Worth More Than Every Single IPO in the Last 45 Years
Three private and newly public companies tied to artificial intelligence now carry a combined valuation that dwarfs decades of tech history, and the profitability math behind those numbers raises serious questions about where the money actually comes from.
The technology market has entered a period where a handful of companies can command valuations that once required an entire industry. The latest example puts today’s AI boom into extraordinary perspective: three companies associated with the technology are collectively valued at more than the combined first-day market value of thousands of U.S. technology IPOs spanning 45 years.
That comparison isn’t perfectly apples-to-apples. But it is still useful because it shows just how much capital investors are willing to place behind the possibility that artificial intelligence will become one of the most valuable technologies in history.
Three Companies, $5.2 Trillion
SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX | SPCX Price Prediction) currently carries a market capitalization of almost $2.1 trillion following its June IPO. The space, AI, and technology company raised $85.7 billion in the offering and finished its first trading day with a market cap similar to its valuation today..
Privately held OpenAI is discussing a new funding round at a valuation of roughly $1.2 trillion, according to Bloomberg. That’s up from the $852 billion valuation attached to its March financing. It recently put its planned IPO on hold after the market began looking askance at the valuations of AI-forward companies.
Finally, privately held Anthropic is reportedly targeting a valuation of about $2 trillion for a potential IPO now anticipated in November (pushed back from an expected October debut).
This chart was put out by the Willett Advisors investment firm’s CEO, Steve Rattner:
I shows the insane valuations being attached to the leading AI stocks compared to the combined first-day market value of 3,365 U.S. technology IPOs from 1980 through 2025 at $4.07 trillion, as compiled by University of Florida professor Jay Ritter. It is a jaw-dropping comparison that pits just three companies against 3,365.
The Valuations Come With a Very Large Asterisk
Yet, it is important not to confuse a fun comparison with an investment metric. Ritter’s historical figures are nominal dollars and represent companies’ market values at their trading prices on the first day following their public debut. SpaceX has a live public-market valuation, while OpenAI’s $1.2 trillion figure is a proposed private financing valuation, and Anthropic’s $2 trillion number is a prospective IPO target.
More importantly, the businesses don’t have comparable financial profiles. OpenAI, for example, projects $278 billion of negative free cash flow from 2026 through 2030, according to the Financial Times. Revenue is forecast to rise from $36 billion in 2026 to $350 billion in 2030, but the company expects to spend about $856 billion on computing infrastructure during that period.
Anthropic faces a similar challenge. The Information reported that it expects revenue to reach as much as $18 billion this year and $55 billion in 2027, but it has pushed back its expected transition to positive cash flow until 2028.
That makes the $5.2 trillion figure less a measure of today’s profits than a bet on tomorrow’s economics.
The AI Bubble Question Gets Harder to Ignore
Ironically, that’s what makes this comparison useful for investors. The market isn’t simply valuing existing earnings. It’s capitalizing enormous expectations for future revenue, margins, and technological breakthroughs.
Yet Apollo Global Management’s chief economist Torsten Slok notes that major technology companies could need to triple their cash flow by 2030 to sustain the industry’s AI infrastructure spending. “If this doesn’t happen, then the risk is that the AI trade weakens, with credit spreads widening, capex plans getting cut and ultimately US GDP growth slowing,” he wrote to clients.
In short, investors are being asked to believe that AI’s future cash generation will eventually catch up with today’s capital requirements.
Key Takeaway
The $5.2 trillion comparison is not proof that AI is a bubble. It is proof that expectations have become enormous.
Smart investors should separate the technology’s potential from the price being paid for it. A revolutionary technology can create extraordinary businesses while investors can still overpay for them. With OpenAI projecting $278 billion in negative free cash flow through 2030 and Anthropic delaying positive cash flow until 2028, profitability remains the number worth watching as these valuations move from private markets to public scrutiny.

articles.summary:
SpaceX, OpenAI, and Anthropic have reached a combined valuation of $5.2 trillion, surpassing the total first-day market value of over 3,300 U.S. technology IPOs from the last 45 years.

### Key Points
- SpaceX currently holds a market capitalization of approximately $2.1 trillion following its June IPO.
- OpenAI is reportedly seeking a $1.2 trillion valuation in its latest private funding round.
- Anthropic is targeting a $2 trillion valuation for a potential IPO now expected in November.
- These three companies’ combined $5.2 trillion valuation exceeds the $4.07 trillion total value of 3,365 U.S. tech IPOs between 1980 and 2025.
- OpenAI projects $278 billion in negative free cash flow between 2026 and 2030 due to massive infrastructure spending.
- Anthropic does not expect to achieve positive cash flow until 2028.

### Why it Matters
These valuations reflect extreme investor optimism regarding the future profitability of artificial intelligence rather than current financial performance. If these companies fail to generate the massive cash flows required to justify their infrastructure costs, the broader technology sector could face significant market volatility and economic headwinds.

articles.title: MoonPay to Acquire North Capital in $60M Deal to Expand Tokenization

articles.summary:
Cryptocurrency payments firm MoonPay has announced an all-stock acquisition of private-markets infrastructure platform North Capital for over $60 million to expand its reach into tokenized assets.

### Key Points
- The deal makes Salt Lake City-based North Capital a wholly owned subsidiary of MoonPay upon regulatory approval.
- North Capital provides regulated financial services and technology for private securities, having processed over $8.7 billion in transaction volume.
- The acquisition includes North Capital’s SEC-registered broker-dealers, a transfer agent, and the PPEX alternative trading system.
- MoonPay is integrating these capabilities to support its Trade platform, which connects financial institutions with tokenized assets and stablecoin liquidity.

### Why it Matters
This acquisition signals MoonPay’s strategic shift from a consumer-facing crypto payments provider toward becoming a comprehensive infrastructure provider for institutional finance. By absorbing North Capital’s regulated framework, the company aims to bridge the gap between traditional private markets and emerging blockchain-based asset tokenization.

articles.title: iPhone Air vs. iPhone 18 Pro Buyer's Guide: Which Should You Buy?
articles.author: Hartley Charlton

The iPhone Air and iPhone 18 Pro are just $100 apart at Apple's current prices, but they offer different advantages. The Air puts a 6.5-inch display in an exceptionally thin, light body. The newer Pro adds a more versatile camera system, longer battery life, and faster performance.
The iPhone Air launched in 2025 at $999, but Apple now sells the 256GB model for $1,099. The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199 for the same storage capacity, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299. Our guide helps to answer the question of how to decide which of these iPhones is best for you.
Both have an Always-On OLED display with ProMotion, Ceramic Shield 2 on the front, an 18-megapixel Center Stage front camera, Wi-Fi 7, and support for Apple Intelligence. Their size differences are as follows:
